01.actor: The father of Shmuel; Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
01.event: A bill of divorce signed by Androlinai of Neharde'a is found; Shmuel's father sends the question to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
01.turn: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia replies that all of Neharde'a must be examined
01.outcome: Not narrated; the passage stops at the instruction
01.summary: A bill of divorce was found in Neharde'a naming Androlinai. Shmuel's father sent the question to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, who replied that all of Neharde'a must be checked for another man of that name.
01.missing: Any examination carried out or what happened to the woman
01.reason: A document is found and a question is sent to a rabbi who rules; coming before the rabbi and his ruling is the only development, and nothing changes afterwards. Cited by Abaye as legal evidence.

02.event: A woman claiming disgust with her husband is compelled by Mar Zutra to stay with him
02.turn: From that couple Rabbi Hanina of Sura is born
02.outcome: The Gemara says the good result was heavenly assistance, not a precedent
02.summary: A woman refused her husband, saying he disgusted her, and Mar Zutra compelled her to remain with him. From that couple Rabbi Hanina of Sura was born. The Gemara adds that this was heavenly help and not a precedent.
02.missing: Detail of the incident itself; it is told in one line
02.reason: There is a ruling that is itself an act (compulsion) and a later change (a great sage is born), but it is told in a single compressed line as legal evidence, with weak narration. Between borderline and story, it sits at borderline; the closing comment is Gemara commentary.

03.missing: Any event beyond a ruling that an L-shaped alleyway needed doors
03.reason: A report of a ruling imposed on an alleyway, followed by analysis of its reasoning; no narrated event or change.

04.event: Rabbi Hanina regularly sends four dinars to a pauper each Shabbat eve; one day he sends them with his wife
04.turn: She returns saying the man does not need charity, having overheard talk of fine tablecloths
04.outcome: The outcome (Rabbi Hanina's response) lies in the following context, not in the passage
04.summary: Rabbi Hanina used to send a poor man four dinars every Shabbat eve. One day he sent them with his wife, who came back and said the man did not need charity; asked why, she began reporting what she overheard in his house.
04.missing: The end of her report and Rabbi Hanina's response, which are in the next segment
04.reason: A habitual frame followed by a one-time event ('one day'), with a discovery that turns the situation; the passage contains the bulk of a story even though its conclusion runs into the next segment.

05.event: Ulla, who used to go up to Eretz Yisrael, dies outside the land
05.turn: Rabbi Elazar, told of it, laments with a verse; told the coffin is coming, he says burial after death is not like being absorbed in life
05.outcome: Ulla's body is brought for burial; Rabbi Elazar's lament stands
05.summary: Ulla, who regularly traveled to Eretz Yisrael, died abroad. When Rabbi Elazar was told, he lamented that Ulla had died in an unclean land; when told his coffin was coming to the land, he replied that being received by the land in death is not like being received in life.
05.reason: There are real events (death abroad, news brought, the coffin being transported) and an emotional response from a rabbi; it is a narrated episode, not a hypothetical or a bare report, though much is dialogue.

06.missing: Any event beyond testimony about a family custom and a reply
06.reason: Rabbi Yehuda ben Gadish's testimony reports a past custom cited as legal evidence and Rabbi Eliezer answers; speech without conflict and a custom that leads nowhere.

07.actor: A dying father and his heirs
07.event: A man wills a palm tree to his daughter, then dies leaving only two half-shares of palm trees
07.turn: The heirs want to give her the two halves
07.outcome: Not in the passage; the following context is a legal question and ruling
07.summary: A man left a palm tree to his daughter in his will, but died owning only two half-trees. The heirs wanted to give her the two halves.
07.missing: Any resolution or change; what follows is a legal discussion
07.reason: A case set up for a ruling: the will and death create a legal question that is then resolved by discussion, with no further narrated action or change.

08.event: Rabbi rules in accordance with Rabbi Elazar
08.outcome: He says Rabbi Elazar may be relied on in exigent circumstances
08.summary: Rabbi once ruled according to Rabbi Elazar; afterwards he remembered that the Sages disagreed and said Rabbi Elazar is worthy to rely on in an emergency.
08.missing: The case ruled on and any consequence
08.reason: A bare report of a ruling and a remark about it, cited as legal evidence; no event beyond ruling and speaking, and nothing follows.

09.actor: Mar Yehuda; residents of Mavrakhta; Rava
09.event: Mar Yehuda finds the residents placing their eiruv in a synagogue and tells them to place it farther in
09.turn: Rava calls him argumentative and says no one follows Rabbi Akiva on eiruvin
09.summary: Mar Yehuda came upon the people of Mavrakhta placing their eiruv in a synagogue and told them to put it farther in to gain distance. Rava rebuked him, saying the law does not follow Rabbi Akiva here.
09.missing: Any action resulting from the instruction or the rebuke
09.reason: A setting that frames a halakhic instruction and a rebuke; the rebuke is ordinary scholarly dispute, and nothing changes.

10.event: Rava, in high spirits, declares himself like ben Azzai ready for any question
10.turn: A Sage tests him with a question about apples for an eiruv, and Rava answers dismissively
10.outcome: Continues in the next segment with the Sage's challenge
10.summary: Rava boasted that he was like ben Azzai in the markets of Tiberias. One of the Sages tested him by asking how many apples are needed for an eiruv, and Rava replied that one does not make an eiruv with apples.
10.missing: How the challenge ends, which is not in the passage
10.reason: All speech, but a boast followed by a test sets up a conflict with implied change (Rava's standing challenged); under R-C2 speech with conflict is borderline.

11.actor: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin
11.event: They buy a maidservant for perutot, lack the money, and leave a piece of silver as collateral
11.turn: Her price rises and the sellers want to back out; the case comes before Rabbi Ami
11.outcome: Rabbi Ami rules there was no acquisition
11.summary: Rav Huna bar Avin's sons agreed to buy a maidservant for copper coins, and having none, left a piece of silver as security. When her value rose, the case came to Rabbi Ami, who ruled that neither coins nor silver had effected the sale.
11.reason: Like the cow case: several narrated actions (purchase, collateral, a price rise that changes the parties' interests) followed by a ruling that resolves them.

12.event: Seven teachings said in Sura before Rav Hisda on Shabbat morning
12.turn: They are repeated the same Shabbat before Rava in Pumbedita
12.outcome: Implied miraculous transmission; discussed in the following context
12.summary: Seven teachings said before Rav Hisda in Sura on Shabbat morning were repeated that afternoon before Rava in Pumbedita, too far to walk on Shabbat.
12.missing: Who carried them and how; the incident is only alluded to as evidence
12.reason: An incident only alluded to as proof, which must be filled in from context (Elijah or a demon); the events are mostly speech, so it is borderline rather than not.

13.actor: Rabbi Ami; Rabbi Yirmeya; Rabbi Zerika
13.event: A dilemma about a runaway slave in a foreign army is put to Rabbi Ami
13.turn: Rabbi Zerika is sent to search the baraitot and finds a parallel, which is questioned
13.outcome: Rabbi Ami sends out a ruling permitting the master to take the slave's value
13.summary: A legal question about a slave who joined a foreign army was put to Rabbi Ami. Rabbi Yirmeya sent Rabbi Zerika to search the sources, he found a baraita about a seized house, and Rabbi Ami then proclaimed a ruling permitting the master to take payment.
13.missing: Any real event beyond question, study and ruling
13.reason: The case is hypothetical and everything that happens is study, question and ruling, which count as speech; there is no conflict and no narrated change.

14.actor: A man who gave a conditional bill of divorce
14.event: He makes the divorce take effect if he does not return within thirty days
14.turn: He arrives on the last day but the ferry is on the other side; he shouts 'see that I have come'
14.outcome: Shmuel rules it is not a return, so the divorce stands
14.summary: A man arranged that his divorce would take effect if he did not return within thirty days. He arrived on time but was stuck on the far bank because the ferry was away, and cried out to people that he had come. Shmuel ruled that this did not count as a return.
14.reason: Several narrated events with tension (condition, journey, the ferry blocking him, his cry) and a ruling that changes his marital status; an incident followed by a ruling, with more than one action.

15.missing: Any event beyond a question and silence
15.reason: Rava poses a scholarly question and Rav Nahman is silent; ordinary scholarly exchange, speech only, no conflict beyond normal discourse.

16.reason: Rav Dimi is silent, Abaye offers an answer and Rav Dimi praises him; standard rabbinic dialogue with no event or conflict.

17.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
17.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba finds Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi hurrying his grandchild to the synagogue with a cheap covering on his head
17.turn: Asked why, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites the verse linking teaching grandchildren to Sinai
17.outcome: From then on Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba would not eat breakfast before teaching his child
17.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba saw Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, carelessly dressed, rushing a child to the synagogue to study, and asked why. He answered with the verse that equates teaching one's grandchildren with standing at Sinai. From then on Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba never ate breakfast before reviewing with his child.
17.reason: An encounter with an observed action, an exchange, and a lasting change in another rabbi's behavior: at least two actions and a change.

18.missing: The incident itself; only its existence and that it was resolved from a mishna are stated
18.reason: An incident is only named, never narrated, and the passage consists of the legal resolution from a mishna; a named-only case brought to a rabbi and resolved is not a story.

19.actor: A blind man who reviewed mishnayot before Mar Shmuel
19.event: One day he is late; Shmuel sends a messenger, who misses him and reaches his house
19.turn: The messenger reports that the man's wife committed adultery
19.outcome: Shmuel tells him to divorce her if he trusts the messenger, and not otherwise
19.summary: A blind man who recited mishnayot for Mar Shmuel was late one day, so Shmuel sent a messenger to fetch him. The two crossed paths, the messenger reached the house and came back saying the man's wife had committed adultery. The blind man asked Shmuel, who told him to divorce her if he trusted the messenger.
19.reason: A one-time event with several actions and a causal chain (lateness, messenger, crossing paths, discovery) leading to a crisis and a ruling.

20.missing: Any response or consequence of Rabbi Akiva's act
20.reason: This is the Yevamot 15a etrog case that the editor ruled 'just a report of what R. Akiva did'; a bare report cited as evidence.
